text: Salmonella covers many types; two mainly affect poultry flocks. Salmonella Pullorum affects chicks, with mortality confined to the first 3 weeks of life — deaths start at 5–7 days, and an early sign is an unusually high number of dead-in-shell chicks and deaths shortly after hatching; surviving chicks show weakness, huddling as if cold, and chalky white/grey diarrhea sticking to the vent. Salmonella in adults causes a septicemic disease with high mortality; layers show dropping egg production and reduced fertility/hatchability. The most typical sign across ages is mucoid yellow-to-green-or-brown diarrhea with strong thirst; Salmonella should always be considered whenever enteritis is seen. Chick Salmonella spreads mainly through the egg (hen to chick), and further through contaminated incubators, chick boxes, premises, feeders, and drinkers. Necropsy findings: chicks dying within 1 week show an unabsorbed yolk sac; those dying within 2 weeks show unabsorbed yolk, peritonitis (cheesy abdominal material), fluid around the heart, an enlarged spleen, and grey necrotic liver spots; in layers, the genital tract can be atrophied/deformed, the spleen enlarged, and the liver takes on a typical bronzed color. Treatment: antibiotics like TMP+Sulfa can reduce mortality but cannot eliminate the disease from the flock entirely.
